hist.q: Which ancient civilisation built the pyramids at Giza?
hist.why: The Egyptians built the pyramids at Giza around 2500 BC as tombs for their kings, the pharaohs.

hist.q: Where did the world's first known writing appear, around 3200 BC?
hist.why: Writing first appeared in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, around 3200 BC: cuneiform marks pressed into clay, first used to keep accounts.

hist.q: Which two rivers gave Mesopotamia its name, "the land between the rivers"?
hist.why: Mesopotamia means "the land between the rivers": the Tigris and Euphrates, in today's Iraq.

hist.q: Which people spread the alphabet that Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts grew from?
hist.why: Phoenician traders, from today's Lebanon, spread an alphabet that became the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.

hist.q: In which country did Buddhism begin?
hist.why: Buddhism began in India around 500 BC with the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha.

hist.q: Which religion began in Arabia in the 600s?
hist.why: Islam began in Arabia in the 600s with the Prophet Muhammad, who died in 632.

hist.q: Which city is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims?
hist.why: Jerusalem is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims, which has made it fought over for centuries.

hist.q: Which Indian emperor backed Buddhism and helped it spread across Asia in the 200s BC?
hist.why: The emperor Ashoka turned to Buddhism after a bloody war around 260 BC and sent missionaries across Asia.

hist.q: Which Roman emperor became Christian and backed the Church in the 300s?
hist.why: Constantine, who ruled from 306 to 337, was the first Christian emperor; Christianity then became Rome's main faith.

hist.q: Which is the world's largest religion by number of followers?
hist.why: Christianity has the most followers, about 2.4 billion, followed by Islam with about 2 billion.

hist.q: Which young king of Macedon conquered the Persian Empire in the 330s BC?
hist.why: Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire and reached India before he died, aged 32, in 323 BC.

hist.q: Which ancient people invented democracy?
hist.why: Democracy, "rule by the people", began in Athens around 500 BC, though only free men could vote.

hist.q: In which year was China first united under one emperor?
hist.why: In 221 BC the state of Qin united China, and its ruler took the title First Emperor.

hist.q: Why do most Chinese people call themselves "Han"?
a: After the Han dynasty, which ruled for four centuries
After a river in northern China
After the first emperor's family name
hist.why: Most Chinese call themselves Han after the Han dynasty, which ruled China from 202 BC to AD 220.

hist.q: Which empire was the largest in the world around 500 BC, stretching from Egypt to India?
hist.why: Around 500 BC the Persian Empire was the largest the world had yet seen, from Egypt to India.

hist.q: What linked China with the Mediterranean for over 1,500 years?
hist.why: The Silk Road, a web of caravan and sea routes, linked China with the Mediterranean from about 130 BC.

hist.q: Which deadly plague spread along trade routes to Europe in the 1340s?
hist.why: The Black Death spread along trade routes from Central Asia and killed about a third of Europe's people in 1347–51.

hist.q: Why did Portugal look for a sea route to Asia around 1500?
a: To buy spices without paying Middle Eastern and Venetian middlemen
hist.why: Portugal sought a sea route to India to buy spices directly, cutting out the middlemen of the Middle East and Venice.

hist.q: Who became Rome's first emperor in 27 BC?
hist.why: Augustus, Julius Caesar's adopted son, became Rome's first emperor in 27 BC.

hist.q: In which year did the last emperor in the West lose his throne, a traditional date for the fall of Rome?
hist.why: In 476 the last Western Roman emperor was deposed; the Eastern, or Byzantine, Empire lasted until 1453.

hist.q: Which city was the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire?
hist.why: Constantinople, today's Istanbul, was the Byzantine capital until the Ottomans took it in 1453.

hist.q: Which modern languages grew out of Latin, Rome's language?
a: Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian
hist.why: Latin grew into the Romance languages: Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.

hist.q: Which empire built Machu Picchu in the Andes?
hist.why: The Inca built Machu Picchu, in today's Peru, in the 1400s; their empire ran along the Andes.

hist.q: Which city was the Aztec capital, where Mexico City stands today?
hist.why: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan stood on a lake where Mexico City is today.

hist.q: What killed most of the native peoples of the Americas after 1492?
a: Diseases brought by Europeans, such as smallpox
Wars between the Aztecs and Inca
hist.why: European diseases such as smallpox, to which Americans had no immunity, killed most of the native population.

hist.q: Who led the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire in 1519–21?
hist.why: Hernán Cortés, with a few hundred Spaniards and thousands of native allies, toppled the Aztecs in 1519–21.

hist.q: Who led the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire from 1532?
hist.why: Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532, during an Inca civil war.

hist.q: In which city was the Prophet Muhammad born?
hist.why: Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570; Mecca is Islam's holiest city.

hist.q: What divides Sunni and Shia Muslims?
a: An early dispute over who should lead the Muslims after Muhammad
Which language the Quran is read in
hist.why: Sunni and Shia Muslims split over who should lead the community after Muhammad: the Shia backed his cousin and son-in-law Ali.

hist.q: How far had Arab armies spread Islamic rule by 750?
hist.why: In the century after 632, Arab armies built an empire from Spain to Central Asia.

hist.q: Which city was the capital of the Abbasid caliphs and a centre of learning from 762?
hist.why: The Abbasids founded Baghdad in 762, and it became one of the world's great centres of learning.

hist.q: Which city did the First Crusade capture in 1099?
hist.why: The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099 and set up crusader states along the eastern Mediterranean.

hist.q: Which Muslim leader retook Jerusalem from the crusaders in 1187?
hist.why: Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, retook Jerusalem in 1187.

hist.q: Which Christian city did the Fourth Crusade sack in 1204?
hist.why: The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople, a Christian city, in 1204, crippling the Byzantine Empire.

hist.q: Who founded the Mongol Empire?
hist.why: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and began the conquests that built the largest land empire in history.

hist.q: Which Mongol ruler conquered all of China and founded the Yuan dynasty?
hist.why: Kublai Khan, Genghis Khan's grandson, completed the conquest of China in 1279 and ruled it as the Yuan dynasty.

hist.q: Which Russian city rose to power by collecting taxes for the Mongols?
hist.why: Moscow grew powerful as tax collector for the Mongol Golden Horde, then threw off Mongol rule in 1480.

hist.q: Which empire captured Constantinople in 1453?
hist.why: The Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.

hist.q: Which country grew out of the heartland of the Ottoman Empire after 1923?
hist.why: After defeat in World War I the Ottoman Empire broke up, and Turkey became a republic in 1923 under Atatürk.

hist.q: The failed Ottoman siege of which city in 1683 marked the start of the empire's retreat?
hist.why: The Ottomans' failed second siege of Vienna in 1683 began their long retreat from Central Europe.

hist.q: Which African country defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896 and kept its independence?
hist.why: Ethiopia beat an Italian army at Adwa in 1896 and stayed independent through the scramble for Africa.

hist.q: Which Southeast Asian country was never colonised by a European power?
hist.why: Thailand, then Siam, stayed independent as a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina.

hist.q: Which country, which has never been a colony, sat as a buffer between British India and the Russian Empire?
hist.why: Afghanistan was a buffer between British India and Russia; Britain controlled its foreign policy from 1879 to 1919.

hist.q: In which year did Columbus first reach the Americas?
hist.why: Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in 1492.

hist.q: Why does Brazil speak Portuguese, when most of South America speaks Spanish?
a: A 1494 treaty gave Portugal the eastern part of South America
Portuguese settlers outnumbered the Spanish everywhere
hist.why: The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 split the New World, giving Portugal the land that became Brazil.

hist.q: Whose expedition was first to sail around the world, in 1519–22?
hist.why: Magellan's Spanish expedition was the first to sail around the world; Magellan himself died on the way.

hist.q: Who was the first European to reach India by sea, in 1498?
hist.why: The Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached India in 1498.

hist.q: About how many enslaved Africans were shipped across the Atlantic?
hist.why: About 12.5 million enslaved Africans were shipped across the Atlantic between the 1500s and the 1860s.

hist.q: Who started the Protestant Reformation in 1517?
hist.why: Martin Luther, a German monk, attacked the sale of indulgences in 1517, splitting Western Christianity.

hist.q: Which invention helped the Reformation spread fast?
hist.why: Gutenberg's printing press, from about 1450, let Luther's writings spread across Europe in weeks.

hist.q: Why did England break with the Pope in the 1530s?
a: The Pope would not let Henry VIII end his marriage
hist.why: Henry VIII broke with Rome when the Pope refused to annul his first marriage, and made himself head of the Church of England.

hist.q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal?
hist.why: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal; it was finished around 1653.

hist.q: Which company took over most of India after the Mughal Empire weakened?
hist.why: After the Mughal Empire broke up, the British East India Company conquered most of India; the British government took over in 1858.

hist.q: Which dynasty, from Manchuria, ruled China from 1644 to 1912?
hist.why: The Manchu Qing dynasty ruled China from 1644 until the 1911 revolution, and pushed its borders to their widest.

hist.q: In which year did the United States declare independence?
hist.why: The thirteen colonies declared independence from Britain on 4 July 1776.

hist.q: Which revolution began with the storming of the Bastille in 1789?
hist.why: The French Revolution began in 1789; the storming of the Bastille prison on 14 July is still France's national day.

hist.q: Which country became the first independent state created by a slave revolt, in 1804?
hist.why: Haiti, once the French colony of Saint-Domingue, became independent in 1804 after a revolt by enslaved people.

hist.q: Who led much of South America to independence from Spain?
hist.why: Simón Bolívar led the wars that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain; Bolivia is named after him.

hist.q: Where was Napoleon finally defeated in 1815?
hist.why: Napoleon was defeated at Waterloo, in today's Belgium, in 1815, and exiled to St Helena.

hist.q: How did Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 help free Spanish America?
a: With Spain's king toppled, colonial elites took power themselves
Napoleon freed the colonies by decree
His army sailed to South America
hist.why: When Napoleon toppled Spain's king in 1808, colonial elites formed their own governments, which led to independence.

hist.q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
hist.why: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s, with machines driven by water and then steam.

hist.q: Which invention powered factories, railways and ships in the Industrial Revolution?
hist.why: James Watt's improved steam engine, from the 1770s, powered factories, then railways and steamships.

hist.q: Which present-day problem began with the burning of coal in the Industrial Revolution?
hist.why: Burning coal, then oil and gas, has raised carbon dioxide in the air since the Industrial Revolution, warming the planet.

hist.q: Which country was united under Prussia's leadership in 1871?
hist.why: Germany was united in 1871 after Prussia's wars with Denmark, Austria and France, led by Otto von Bismarck.

hist.q: Which country was united in 1861, led by figures like Garibaldi?
hist.why: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861; Rome joined in 1870.

hist.q: Why is Bolivia landlocked today?
a: Chile took its coast in the War of the Pacific (1879–84)
It sold its coast to Peru
An earthquake cut it off from the sea
It was never given a coast at independence
hist.why: Chile took Bolivia's coastline in the War of the Pacific of 1879–84, leaving Bolivia landlocked.

hist.q: Which country had the largest empire in history, at its height around 1920?
hist.why: At its height around 1920, the British Empire ruled about a quarter of the world's land and people.

hist.q: Which European country ruled India until 1947?
hist.why: Britain ruled India, directly from 1858 and through the East India Company before that, until independence in 1947.

hist.q: What was the "Scramble for Africa"?
a: The rush by European powers to colonise Africa, about 1880–1914
A race to find the source of the Nile
African kingdoms competing for trade with India
The end of the slave trade
hist.why: In the Scramble for Africa, about 1880–1914, European powers seized almost all of Africa.

hist.q: Who personally owned the Congo as a colony from 1885 to 1908?
hist.why: King Leopold II of Belgium ruled the Congo as his own property; millions died under forced labour before Belgium took it over in 1908.

hist.q: Which European country ruled Algeria from 1830 to 1962?
hist.why: France ruled Algeria from 1830 and treated it as part of France; it won independence in 1962 after a long war.

hist.q: Which country colonised Indonesia?
hist.why: The Dutch ruled Indonesia, the Dutch East Indies, for over three centuries until 1949.

hist.q: Which two African countries were never colonised?
hist.why: By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia in Africa were independent; every other country was ruled by a European power.

hist.q: What event set off World War I in 1914?
a: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo
hist.why: A Bosnian Serb nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo in June 1914.

hist.q: Which two countries were Germany's main allies in World War I?
hist.why: Germany fought alongside Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria, the Central Powers.

hist.q: Which side won World War I?
a: The Allies: Britain, France, Russia, Italy and the US
The Central Powers: Germany and Austria-Hungary
Neither: it ended in a draw
hist.why: The Allies, led by Britain and France, and joined by the US in 1917, defeated the Central Powers in November 1918.

hist.q: Why did Britain enter World War I?
a: To win back colonies from France
hist.why: Britain declared war in August 1914 after Germany marched through neutral Belgium to attack France.

hist.q: Which treaty, signed in 1919, punished Germany after World War I?
hist.why: The Treaty of Versailles took land from Germany, limited its army and made it pay reparations; many Germans resented it.

hist.q: Which four empires collapsed because of World War I?
hist.why: World War I destroyed four empires: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman.

hist.q: Why did the United States join World War I in 1917?
hist.why: The US joined in April 1917 after German submarines attacked American shipping, and Germany secretly courted Mexico.

hist.q: What was the Russian Revolution of 1917?
a: The overthrow of the tsar, then a Communist takeover led by Lenin
A rebellion of Russian colonies in Asia
A peasant revolt that restored the tsar
hist.why: In 1917 Russians overthrew Tsar Nicholas II; that November Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power and later founded the Soviet Union.

hist.q: Who led Nazi Germany?
hist.why: Adolf Hitler led the Nazi Party and ruled Germany as dictator from 1933 to 1945.

hist.q: Who was the fascist dictator of Italy from 1922?
hist.why: Benito Mussolini took power in Italy in 1922 and created the first fascist state.

hist.q: What was the Great Depression?
a: A worldwide economic collapse that began in 1929
A long period of cold weather in the 1930s
A disease that spread after World War I
hist.why: The Great Depression began with the Wall Street crash of 1929; by 1932 about a quarter of American and German workers had no job.

hist.q: Who ruled the Soviet Union as dictator from the late 1920s until 1953?
hist.why: Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until his death in 1953; millions died in his purges and famines.

hist.q: What was "appeasement" in the 1930s?
a: Giving in to Hitler's demands to avoid war
An alliance between Britain and the USSR
Sending aid to Germany during the Depression
hist.why: Britain and France gave in to Hitler's demands, as at Munich in 1938, hoping to avoid another world war.

hist.q: What secret deal let Hitler invade Poland in 1939 without fighting the Soviet Union?
hist.why: In August 1939 Hitler and Stalin signed a pact not to fight each other and secretly agreed to split Poland.

hist.q: Who won the Spanish Civil War of 1936–39?
hist.why: General Franco's Nationalists, helped by Hitler and Mussolini, won the Spanish Civil War; Franco ruled Spain until 1975.

hist.q: Which event started World War II in Europe?
hist.why: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war two days later.

hist.q: Which three countries led the Axis in World War II?
hist.why: Germany, Italy and Japan were the main Axis powers.

hist.q: Which three countries led the Allies to victory in World War II?
a: Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States
hist.why: The "Big Three" Allies were Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States, joined by China and many others.

hist.q: Which attack brought the United States into World War II?
a: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941
hist.why: Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on 7 December 1941; the US then entered the war.

hist.q: What was the Holocaust?
a: The Nazis' murder of about six million Jews
A famine in the Soviet Union
hist.why: In the Holocaust, Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, along with Roma and others.

hist.q: Which two Japanese cities were hit by atomic bombs in 1945?
hist.why: The US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945; Japan surrendered days later.

hist.q: Which side was Italy on at the start of World War II?
hist.why: Mussolini's Italy fought with Germany from 1940; after Mussolini fell in 1943, Italy switched to the Allies.

hist.q: Which country stayed neutral throughout World War II?
hist.why: Switzerland, along with Sweden, Spain, Portugal and Ireland, stayed neutral; Belgium, Norway and Greece were invaded.

hist.q: What was D-Day?
a: The Allied landing in Normandy, France, on 6 June 1944
Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union
hist.why: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, Allied troops landed in Normandy and began freeing Western Europe.

hist.q: Which battle in 1942–43 turned the war against Germany in the east?
hist.why: The German Sixth Army was surrounded and surrendered at Stalingrad in early 1943, a turning point of the war.

hist.q: Why did Japan go to war with the United States in 1941?
a: It wanted an empire in Asia, and the US had cut off its oil
hist.why: Japan wanted an Asian empire; when the US cut off its oil in 1941, Japan struck Pearl Harbor and seized oil-rich Southeast Asia.

hist.q: Which international organisation was founded in 1945 to keep the peace?
hist.why: The United Nations was founded in 1945, replacing the failed League of Nations.

hist.q: Which country was split into East and West after World War II?
hist.why: Germany was split into West Germany and Soviet-run East Germany in 1949; it reunited in 1990.

hist.q: Which country, invaded by Germany in 1941, lost the most people in World War II?
hist.why: The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people, more than any other country.

hist.q: Which battle in 1942 turned the Pacific war against Japan?
hist.why: At Midway in June 1942, the US sank four Japanese aircraft carriers, turning the tide in the Pacific.

hist.q: Which Allied country fought Japan from 1937, losing about 15 to 20 million people?
hist.why: China fought Japan from 1937 to 1945 and lost about 15 to 20 million people.

hist.q: Who led India's non-violent campaign for independence?
hist.why: Mahatma Gandhi led mass non-violent protests against British rule; India won independence in 1947.

hist.q: Which country was created when British India was partitioned in 1947?
hist.why: In 1947 British India was split into India and Pakistan; East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971.

hist.q: Which region have India and Pakistan disputed since 1947?
hist.why: India and Pakistan have fought over Kashmir since partition in 1947; it remains divided.

hist.q: Which country ruled Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia as Indochina?
hist.why: France ruled Indochina until its defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.

hist.q: Which country ruled Korea from 1910 to 1945?
hist.why: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it until its defeat in 1945; Korea was then divided.

hist.q: Which country ruled the Philippines from 1898 to 1946?
hist.why: The US took the Philippines from Spain in 1898 and granted independence in 1946, after Japanese occupation.

hist.q: Which British colony was handed back to China in 1997?
hist.why: Britain returned Hong Kong to China in 1997; Portugal returned Macau in 1999.

hist.q: Which two superpowers were rivals in the Cold War?
a: The United States and the Soviet Union
hist.why: The Cold War, from about 1947 to 1991, was a rivalry between the US and the Soviet Union and their allies.

hist.q: What was the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962?
a: A standoff over Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba that nearly caused nuclear war
A US invasion that overthrew Fidel Castro
A fight over Cuba's sugar exports
hist.why: In October 1962 the US found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba; after 13 tense days, the Soviets removed them and the US quietly pulled its missiles from Turkey.

hist.q: What did the Berlin Wall divide?
a: Communist East Berlin from West Berlin
Berlin from the rest of Germany
hist.why: East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop its people fleeing west; it was opened in 1989.

hist.q: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
hist.why: The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989; Germany reunited in 1990.

hist.q: What is NATO?
a: A military alliance of the US, Canada and European countries, founded in 1949
hist.why: NATO was founded in 1949 to defend Western Europe; an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

hist.q: Who were the two sides in the Vietnam War?
a: Communist North Vietnam against US-backed South Vietnam
hist.why: Communist North Vietnam and its southern guerrillas fought US-backed South Vietnam; the North won in 1975.

hist.q: What caused the Vietnam War?
a: Vietnam was split in 1954, and the US tried to stop the communist North uniting it
A dispute over oil in the South China Sea
France and the US fought over Vietnam
hist.why: After France left in 1954, Vietnam was divided; the US backed the South to "contain" communism, and fought there from 1965 to 1973.

hist.q: Which country was split along the 38th parallel after 1945?
hist.why: Korea was split at the 38th parallel in 1945; the Korean War of 1950–53 ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty.

hist.q: Who started the Korean War in 1950?
a: North Korea, by invading the South
South Korea, by invading the North
hist.why: Communist North Korea invaded the South in June 1950; a UN force led by the US fought back, and China joined the North.

hist.q: What was the Iron Curtain?
a: The line dividing communist Eastern Europe from the West
hist.why: Churchill called the divide between Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe and the West an "Iron Curtain" in 1946.

hist.q: Which alliance did the Soviet Union lead in Eastern Europe?
hist.why: The Soviet Union led the Warsaw Pact, founded in 1955; it dissolved in 1991.

hist.q: What was the Marshall Plan?
a: American aid to rebuild Western Europe after World War II
A US plan to land on the Moon
hist.why: From 1948 the US gave about $13 billion in Marshall Plan aid to rebuild Western Europe and keep communism out.

hist.q: Who led the 1959 revolution that made Cuba communist?
hist.why: Fidel Castro overthrew the dictator Batista in 1959 and allied Cuba with the Soviet Union.

hist.q: Why did the US and the Soviet Union never fight each other directly?
a: Both had nuclear weapons, so a direct war could destroy them both
They had signed a peace treaty
hist.why: With nuclear weapons on both sides, direct war risked mutual destruction, so they fought through proxy wars instead.

hist.q: Which country did the Soviet Union invade in 1979, starting a ten-year war?
hist.why: The Soviets invaded Afghanistan in 1979 and withdrew in 1989 after a costly war against US-backed rebels.

hist.q: In which year did the Vietnam War end with the fall of Saigon?
hist.why: North Vietnamese troops took Saigon in April 1975, and Vietnam was united under communist rule.

hist.q: Which first did the Soviet Union achieve in 1957, starting the space race?
a: Sending the first woman into space
hist.why: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite, in 1957; the US landed on the Moon in 1969.

hist.q: In which year was the state of Israel founded?
hist.why: Israel declared independence in 1948 as British rule in Palestine ended; war with its Arab neighbours followed.

hist.q: Which territories did Israel capture in the 1967 Six-Day War?
a: The West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and Sinai
hist.why: In the 1967 war Israel took the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and Sinai; it returned Sinai to Egypt by 1982.

hist.q: Which country ruled Palestine between the two world wars?
hist.why: Britain ruled Palestine under a League of Nations mandate from 1920 to 1948.

hist.q: Which revolution in 1979 turned Iran into an Islamic republic?
a: The Iranian Revolution, led by Ayatollah Khomeini
hist.why: In 1979 Iranians overthrew the Shah, and Ayatollah Khomeini founded the Islamic Republic.

hist.q: Why have outside powers long competed for influence in the Middle East?
a: It holds nearly half the world's proven oil
It has the world's largest population
It has most of the world's gold
hist.why: The Middle East holds nearly half the world's proven oil reserves, and key shipping routes such as the Suez Canal.

hist.q: Who led the Communists to victory in China in 1949?
hist.why: Mao Zedong founded the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949.

hist.q: Where did China's Nationalist government flee after losing the civil war in 1949?
hist.why: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists fled to Taiwan, which is still governed separately from mainland China.

hist.q: Which leader opened China's economy to markets and foreign investment from 1978?
hist.why: Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978 led to decades of fast growth that lifted about 800 million people out of poverty.

hist.q: What was the Great Leap Forward?
a: Mao's 1958 push to industrialise fast, which caused a famine that killed tens of millions
A long march by the Red Army
China's entry into the World Trade Organization
hist.why: Mao's Great Leap Forward, from 1958, forced farmers into communes and backyard steel-making; the famine that followed killed tens of millions.

hist.q: What was the Cultural Revolution of 1966–76?
a: Mao's campaign against "old" ideas, when Red Guards attacked teachers and officials
A boom in Chinese films and music
hist.why: In the Cultural Revolution, Mao turned young Red Guards against teachers, officials and old traditions; hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, died.

hist.q: Which country voted to leave the European Union in 2016?
hist.why: Britain voted to leave the EU in 2016 and left in 2020, the first country to do so.

hist.q: Why was the European project started in the 1950s?
a: To make another war between France and Germany impossible
To defeat the Soviet Union in war
hist.why: Pooling coal and steel, the industries of war, was meant to bind France and Germany so they could never fight again.

hist.q: What is the euro?
a: The shared currency of most EU countries
hist.why: The euro, launched in 1999, is used by about 20 EU countries.

hist.q: Who became South Africa's first Black president in 1994, after apartheid ended?
hist.why: Nelson Mandela, jailed for 27 years, became president in 1994 after South Africa's first all-race election.

hist.q: What was apartheid?
a: South Africa's system of racial segregation, 1948–1994
A war between Egypt and Sudan
hist.why: Apartheid was South Africa's system of laws separating people by race, from 1948 until the early 1990s.

hist.q: Which was the first British colony in Black Africa to win independence, in 1957?
hist.why: Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, won independence in 1957 and inspired the rest of Africa.

hist.q: Which country did Nigeria win independence from in 1960?
hist.why: Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, became independent from Britain in 1960.

hist.q: Why do many African countries have straight-line borders?
a: European powers drew them on maps, often ignoring the peoples living there
They follow lines of latitude chosen by Africans
They were drawn by the United Nations
hist.why: Most African borders were drawn by European powers, especially at the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, and kept at independence.

hist.q: Which European country ruled Angola and Mozambique until 1975?
hist.why: Portugal held on to Angola and Mozambique until 1975, after long wars of independence.

hist.q: What happened in Rwanda in 1994?
a: A genocide in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed
hist.why: In 1994 Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days.

hist.q: In which year did the Soviet Union break up?
hist.why: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 into 15 independent countries.

hist.q: Which Soviet leader's reforms helped end the Cold War?
hist.why: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms, glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), loosened Soviet control and helped end the Cold War.

hist.q: How many countries emerged from the Soviet Union?
hist.why: Fifteen republics became independent, including Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan and the three Baltic states.

hist.q: Which three Baltic countries broke away from the Soviet Union first?
hist.why: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, annexed by Stalin in 1940, led the way out of the Soviet Union in 1990–91; all are now in the EU and NATO.

hist.q: Which country broke apart in a series of wars in the 1990s?
hist.why: Yugoslavia broke apart in wars from 1991; Czechoslovakia split peacefully in 1993.

hist.q: Where did the worst massacre in Europe since World War II take place, in 1995?
hist.why: Bosnian Serb forces killed about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in July 1995.

hist.q: Which country split peacefully in two in 1993?
hist.why: Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, the "Velvet Divorce".

hist.q: Which is the world's newest country, independent since 2011?
hist.why: South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war.

hist.q: Which country became independent from Indonesia in 2002?
hist.why: East Timor, a former Portuguese colony invaded by Indonesia in 1975, voted for independence in 1999 and became independent in 2002.

hist.q: Which country was expelled from Malaysia and became independent in 1965?
hist.why: Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963 but was expelled in 1965, and grew into one of the richest countries in the world.

hist.q: Which country did the United States invade weeks after the 11 September 2001 attacks?
hist.why: After 9/11 the US invaded Afghanistan, where al-Qaeda was based; it invaded Iraq in 2003.

hist.q: Which country did Russia invade in full in February 2022?
hist.why: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the largest war in Europe since 1945.

hist.q: What was the Arab Spring of 2011?
a: A wave of protests against rulers across the Arab world
A peace deal between Israel and its neighbours
hist.why: In 2011 protests swept the Arab world; rulers fell in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen, and Syria fell into civil war.

hist.q: Which group carried out the 11 September 2001 attacks on the United States?
hist.why: Al-Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden, carried out the 9/11 attacks, killing almost 3,000 people.

hist.q: Which peninsula did Russia annex from Ukraine in 2014?
hist.why: Russia seized and annexed Crimea in 2014; most of the world still considers it part of Ukraine.

hist.q: Which country's civil war, from 2011, created the largest refugee crisis of its time?
hist.why: Syria's civil war drove over 13 million people from their homes; the Assad government fell in December 2024.

hist.q: Which country has had the world's largest population since 2023?
hist.why: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023, with over 1.4 billion people.

hist.q: Which country emits the most carbon dioxide today?
hist.why: China emits the most CO2, about a third of the world total, followed by the United States and India.

hist.q: Where is most of the world's population growth expected until 2050?
hist.why: More than half of the world's population growth to 2050 is expected in Africa, which has the youngest population.

hist.q: Why did farming let some people stop growing food?
a: Farmers produced a surplus that could feed others
hist.why: A surplus of grain could feed priests, craftsmen, soldiers and rulers.

hist.q: Where was writing first invented?
a: Sumer, in what is now Iraq
hist.why: Writing appeared in Sumer around 3200 BC, and in Egypt at about the same time.

hist.q: What are oracle bones?
a: Bones carved with the oldest Chinese writing
Tools used to build the pyramids
hist.why: Shang kings used them to ask their ancestors questions; the carvings are the oldest Chinese script.

hist.q: According to the Buddha, what causes suffering?
hist.why: He taught that suffering comes from craving, and that it can be ended.

hist.q: What did Athens begin in 508 BC?
hist.why: Citizens voted on laws directly: the first democracy.

hist.q: Who first united China, in 221 BC?
hist.why: He ended the Warring States period and standardised writing, coins and weights.

hist.q: Where does our system of numbers, with zero, come from?
hist.why: Indian mathematicians developed decimal place value and zero.

hist.q: What made long sea voyages across the Indian Ocean predictable?
hist.why: The monsoon blows one way in summer and the other in winter.

hist.q: Who was Mansa Musa?
a: A ruler of Mali famed for his gold
hist.why: His 1324 pilgrimage spread Mali’s fame to Europe and the Middle East.

hist.q: What were Roman roads mainly built for?
hist.why: They moved the legions, and with them trade and ideas.

hist.q: How did the Inca keep records without writing?
hist.why: Coloured, knotted strings recorded numbers such as taxes and census counts.

hist.q: Why is 622 year one of the Islamic calendar?
a: Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina
hist.why: The Hijra, the move to Medina, began the Muslim community.

hist.q: Where does the word 'algorithm' come from?
a: The name of the mathematician al-Khwarizmi
hist.why: Al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad in the 800s; his book also gave us the word algebra.

hist.q: What did Magna Carta establish?
a: That even the king must obey the law
That England would become a republic
hist.why: It was a landmark for the idea of limited government.

hist.q: Who called the First Crusade in 1095?
hist.why: He called it at Clermont in France.

hist.q: How did the Mongols usually treat a city that surrendered without a fight?
hist.why: Surrender usually meant survival; resistance often meant destruction.

hist.q: Which city did Hülegü sack in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate?
hist.why: The sack of Baghdad was one of the great catastrophes of the medieval Islamic world.

hist.q: Who conquered Constantinople in 1453?
hist.why: His cannon broke the city’s walls, ending the Byzantine Empire.

hist.q: What was the first voyage around the world?
a: Vasco da Gama's voyage to India
hist.why: Magellan died on the way, but one ship made it home in 1522.

hist.q: Which country received the most enslaved Africans?
hist.why: Almost 5 million were taken to Brazil, the last country in the Americas to end slavery, in 1888.

hist.q: What did Gutenberg’s printing press do?
a: Made books cheap and fast to produce
hist.why: It spread ideas faster than ever before.

hist.q: What did Luther attack in his 95 theses?
hist.why: Indulgences promised less punishment after death in return for money.

hist.q: Why did Henry VIII break with the Pope?
a: The Pope would not end his marriage
He wanted to join the Ottomans
hist.why: Refused an annulment, Henry made himself head of the Church of England in 1534.

hist.q: What did Copernicus argue in 1543?
a: The Earth goes around the Sun
hist.why: This heliocentric idea overturned 1,400 years of belief.

hist.q: Who held real power in Tokugawa Japan?
hist.why: The emperor reigned; the shogun ruled.

hist.q: What did Watt's steam engine make possible?
a: Factories that did not need to be beside rivers
hist.why: Steam power freed factories from waterwheels; later it drove trains and ships.

hist.q: Which was the first country to give women the vote?
hist.why: New Zealand, in 1893.

hist.q: Which idea did John Locke argue for?
a: Government rests on the consent of the people
hist.why: Jefferson echoed him in the Declaration of Independence.

hist.q: What did the American colonists object to?
a: Being taxed without a say in Parliament
hist.why: 'No taxation without representation.'

hist.q: Who united Germany through "blood and iron"?
hist.why: Bismarck’s wars against Denmark, Austria and France created the German Empire in 1871.

hist.q: What did the Suez Canal link?
a: The Mediterranean and the Red Sea
The Black Sea and the Baltic
The Indian Ocean and the Pacific
hist.why: It opened in 1869 and greatly shortened the route to India.

hist.q: Where was Archduke Franz Ferdinand assassinated?
hist.why: He was shot there on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip.

hist.q: When did the fighting in World War I end?
hist.why: The armistice came into force at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.

hist.q: Which of these countries was created after World War I?
hist.why: Poland was reborn in 1918 after more than a century of partition.

hist.q: Who led the Bolshevik revolution in 1917?
hist.why: Lenin led the Bolsheviks; Stalin took over after his death in 1924.

hist.q: What was the Munich Agreement of 1938?
a: Britain and France let Germany take the Sudetenland
Germany and the Soviet Union agreed to split Poland
The treaty that ended World War I
An alliance between Germany and Japan
hist.why: It was the high point of appeasement.

hist.q: What did Hitler mean by Lebensraum, or 'living space'?
a: Land to be conquered in eastern Europe for Germans
A neutral zone between Germany and France
hist.why: Hitler planned to seize land in Poland and the Soviet Union, and to remove or enslave the people living there.

hist.q: How did the German army get around France's main defences in 1940?
a: By sea across the English Channel
hist.why: France's Maginot Line forts guarded the border, but German tanks went through the Ardennes, which the French thought impassable.

hist.q: Why was invading the Soviet Union such a gamble for Germany?
a: Britain was still undefeated, so Germany now fought on two fronts
The Soviet Union was a German ally with a huge army
Germany had no tanks left after France
The US had already joined the war
hist.why: With Britain still fighting in the west, Germany now faced the two-front war it had tried to avoid in 1939.

hist.q: Where did the Nazis build the main death camps?
a: In the Soviet Union's far east
hist.why: Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Bełżec, Sobibor and Chełmno were all in occupied Poland.

hist.q: When did World War II end in Europe?
hist.why: Germany surrendered in early May 1945, a week after Hitler's suicide; 8 May is VE Day.

hist.q: How did Gandhi oppose British rule?
a: By asking the Soviet Union to invade
hist.why: Boycotts, strikes and marches such as the Salt March.

hist.q: Why was it called a "cold" war?
a: The superpowers never fought each other directly
It was fought mainly in the Arctic
hist.why: They competed through arms, alliances and proxy wars instead.

hist.q: Where did the Soviet Union place nuclear missiles in 1962?
hist.why: The discovery set off the Cuban Missile Crisis.

hist.q: When did the Berlin Wall open?
hist.why: It opened on 9 November 1989; Germany reunited in 1990.

hist.q: What did Israel take in the 1967 Six-Day War?
a: The West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem, Golan and Sinai
hist.why: Sinai was later returned to Egypt after the 1979 peace.

hist.q: What happened in the Great Leap Forward?
a: A famine that killed tens of millions
hist.why: Forced communes and false reports led to the deadliest famine in history.

hist.q: Why did France and West Germany pool their coal and steel in 1951?
a: To make war between France and Germany impossible
To sell coal to the US
To fight the Soviet Union directly
hist.why: Shared control of the raw materials of war bound former enemies together.

hist.q: Which country was the first to leave the EU?
hist.why: Norway and Switzerland never joined; Britain left in 2020.

hist.q: What was Solidarity?
a: A free trade union in communist Poland
hist.why: Founded in 1980 at the Gdańsk shipyard.

hist.q: What happened at Srebrenica in 1995?
a: About 8,000 Muslim men and boys were murdered
hist.why: It was ruled a genocide by international courts.

hist.q: When did Russia launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine?
hist.why: It had annexed Crimea in 2014.

hist.q: Why did the first civilisations grow up beside great rivers?
a: Rivers gave water and fertile soil for farming
Rivers protected them from all invaders
Rivers were the only source of stone
hist.why: Irrigated, silt-rich land fed large populations; organising the water gave rulers power.

hist.q: Why did writing first develop in Mesopotamia?
a: To keep records of grain, animals and taxes
To write down poetry and songs
To record the words of prophets
hist.why: The earliest cuneiform tablets are accounts kept by temples and palaces.

hist.q: What do Judaism, Christianity and Islam have in common?
a: Belief in one God and in Abraham as a founding father
hist.why: They are called the Abrahamic faiths.

hist.q: What is the core idea of karma, in Hinduism and Buddhism?
a: Actions have consequences in this life or the next
There is one God who judges the dead
Suffering is caused by the gods
hist.why: Karma ties actions to rebirth.

hist.q: Why is ancient Athens remembered as the birthplace of democracy?
a: Male citizens voted directly on laws in an assembly
It elected a king every year
Everyone, including slaves and women, could vote
It was the first republic with a president
hist.why: Direct democracy began there in 508 BC, though women, slaves and foreigners were excluded.

hist.q: Which philosopher tutored the young Alexander the Great?
hist.why: Aristotle was a student of Plato, who was a student of Socrates.

hist.q: What was the main difference between the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
a: In the empire, one emperor held supreme power
The republic was ruled by the Pope
hist.why: Augustus kept the republic’s forms but ruled as emperor from 27 BC.

hist.q: Which modern languages grew out of Latin?
a: Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian
hist.why: They are called the Romance languages.

hist.q: What divides Sunni and Shia Muslims?
a: A dispute over who should lead the Muslim community after Muhammad
hist.why: Shia Muslims held that leadership belonged to Muhammad’s family, through Ali.

hist.q: What was feudalism?
a: A system where land was granted in return for loyalty and service
hist.why: Kings, lords, knights and peasants each owed service to someone above them.

hist.q: How did the Black Death change life for European peasants who survived?
a: Labour became scarce, so they could demand higher wages
They were all made into knights
Serfdom became stricter everywhere in Europe
hist.why: With a third or more of Europe dead, workers had more bargaining power.

hist.q: What was the aim of the Crusades?
a: To take Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule
To find a sea route to India
hist.why: The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099; Muslims retook it in 1187.

hist.q: What does 'Renaissance' mean, and what was reborn?
a: 'Rebirth': the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome
hist.why: It began in Italy around 1400.

hist.q: What was the Protestant Reformation?
a: A split from the Catholic Church that created Protestant churches
A reform of the Roman army
A revolt of peasants against kings
hist.why: It began with Luther in 1517 and divided Western Christianity.

hist.q: What was new about the Scientific Revolution?
a: Ideas were tested by observation, experiment and mathematics
Scientists relied only on ancient books
It was the first time anyone studied the stars
hist.why: Copernicus, Galileo and Newton changed how humans understand nature.

hist.q: What did Newton's law of universal gravitation explain?
a: The same force makes apples fall and keeps planets in orbit
hist.why: Newton published it in 1687.

hist.q: What was the Enlightenment?
a: An 18th-century movement arguing that reason should guide society and government
A school of painting in Italy
hist.why: Its ideas inspired the American and French revolutions.

hist.q: What did the French Revolution's slogan 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity' express?
a: Rights for all citizens instead of privileges for nobles and clergy
hist.why: It began in 1789 and abolished the monarchy in 1792.

hist.q: Why did Spain’s American colonies begin to break away after 1808?
a: Napoleon invaded Spain, so the colonies began governing themselves
hist.why: Bolívar and San Martín then led the wars of independence.

hist.q: What was the Columbian Exchange?
a: The transfer of crops, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world
A trade deal between Spain and Portugal
A treaty ending the slave trade
hist.why: Potatoes and maize spread worldwide; smallpox devastated the Americas.

hist.q: Why did most native people of the Americas die after 1492?
a: European diseases such as smallpox, to which they had no immunity
They were all killed in battle
hist.why: Disease killed perhaps up to 90% in a century.

hist.q: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain?
a: It had coal, capital, markets and high wages that made machines pay
It had the largest population in the world
Its king ordered factories to be built
hist.why: Cheap coal and expensive labour made mechanisation profitable.

hist.q: How did the Industrial Revolution change where people lived?
a: Millions moved from farms to factory cities
People moved from cities to farms
hist.why: By 1901 about three in four people in England and Wales lived in towns.

hist.q: What is nationalism?
a: The idea that a people sharing a culture should rule itself in its own state
Loyalty to the Church above all
The belief that empires keep peace
hist.why: It united Germany and Italy and broke up multinational empires.

hist.q: What was the Scramble for Africa?
a: The rapid division of Africa among European powers, about 1880–1914
A gold rush in South Africa
hist.why: By 1914 Europeans ruled about nine-tenths of Africa.

hist.q: What made it possible for Europeans to conquer inland Africa after 1880?
a: Medicine against malaria, steamboats and machine guns
The end of the slave trade
hist.why: Quinine, steam and firepower gave them new reach.

hist.q: Why did a single assassination in 1914 lead to a world war?
a: Alliances pulled the great powers in one after another
Everyone wanted to avenge the archduke
hist.why: Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia, Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria, and so on.

hist.q: Why did trench warfare cause so many deaths for so little ground?
a: Machine guns and artillery made attacking across open ground deadly
The trenches were in the Arctic
hist.why: The Western Front barely moved from late 1914 to 1918.

hist.q: Which four empires collapsed because of World War I?
hist.why: New nation-states replaced them across Europe and the Middle East.

hist.q: How did the Great Depression help Hitler come to power?
a: Mass unemployment made desperate voters turn to extremists
It ended the Treaty of Versailles
hist.why: By 1932 about six million Germans were out of work.

hist.q: What did communism and fascism have in common?
a: Both were one-party dictatorships that crushed opposition
Both were founded in the US
hist.why: They differed in ideas but both used terror and propaganda.

hist.q: What was appeasement?
a: Giving in to Hitler’s demands in the hope of avoiding war
hist.why: It peaked at Munich in 1938 and failed in 1939.

hist.q: Why is Stalingrad seen as a turning point of World War II?
a: A whole German army was destroyed and Germany began retreating in the east
It was where the US entered the war
It ended the war in the Pacific
It was the first use of the atomic bomb
hist.why: About 91,000 Germans surrendered in February 1943.

hist.q: Why was the United Nations created in 1945?
a: To keep the peace and prevent another world war
hist.why: Its five permanent Security Council members were the main winners.

hist.q: What was containment?
a: The US policy of stopping communism from spreading
A Soviet plan to build the Berlin Wall
hist.why: It shaped US policy from 1947: the Marshall Plan, NATO, Korea and Vietnam.

hist.q: What was 'mutually assured destruction'?
a: The idea that a nuclear attack would destroy both sides, so neither would start one
A treaty to destroy all weapons
hist.why: It kept the superpowers from fighting each other directly.

hist.q: What was a proxy war in the Cold War?
a: A war where the superpowers backed opposite sides without fighting each other directly
A war fought only at sea
A civil war inside the US
hist.why: Angola, Afghanistan and Nicaragua are examples.

hist.q: Why did Asian colonies win independence soon after 1945?
a: The war had weakened Europe, and Japan had shown colonial rulers could be beaten
The UN ordered all empires closed in 1945
Britain lost a war to India
hist.why: India, Indonesia, the Philippines and Burma were independent by 1949.

hist.q: Why were many independent African states unstable at first?
a: Colonial borders lumped rival groups together and economies relied on a few exports
They were still ruled by Europe
hist.why: Coups and civil wars were common in the decades after 1960.

hist.q: What was apartheid?
a: South Africa's system of laws separating people by race
hist.why: It lasted from 1948 until Mandela’s election in 1994.

hist.q: Why has the Middle East drawn so much outside involvement since 1945?
a: It holds nearly half the world’s proven oil
It is the most populous region
It has the world’s largest armies
It produces most of the world’s food
hist.why: Oil made the Gulf central to world politics.

hist.q: What were Deng Xiaoping's reforms from 1978?
a: Opening China to markets and foreign investment while the Party kept power
A return to the Cultural Revolution
hist.why: China grew about 10% a year for three decades.

hist.q: What is the EU’s single market?
a: Goods, services, money and people move freely between members
All members use the same army
All taxes are paid to Brussels
hist.why: It grew from the 1957 common market.

hist.q: Why did the Soviet Union collapse in 1991?
a: A failing economy, reforms that loosened control and rising nationalism in its republics
It lost a war with the US
Its leader was overthrown by NATO
hist.why: All fifteen republics became independent countries.

hist.q: What caused the 2008 financial crisis?
a: Banks lent heavily on risky home loans that could not be repaid
hist.why: Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008.

hist.q: What was the Arab Spring?
a: A wave of uprisings across the Arab world in 2011
A peace treaty between Israel and its neighbours
An oil boom in the Gulf
hist.why: Rulers fell in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen; Syria slid into civil war.

geo.q: Which river flows through Egypt?
geo.why: The Nile flows north through Egypt to the Mediterranean; almost all Egyptians live along it.

geo.q: Which river carries the most water in the world?
geo.why: The Amazon carries more water than the next seven largest rivers combined, mostly through Brazil.

geo.q: Which is the longest river in Asia?
geo.why: The Yangtze, about 6,300 km long, flows across China to the sea at Shanghai.

geo.q: Which river is sacred to Hindus?
geo.why: Hindus consider the Ganges sacred; millions bathe in it at Varanasi and at the Kumbh Mela festival.

geo.q: Which river flows through the middle of the United States to the Gulf of Mexico?
geo.why: The Mississippi and its tributaries drain about 40% of the United States.

geo.q: Which two rivers flow through Iraq?
geo.why: The Tigris and Euphrates flow through Iraq to the Persian Gulf; ancient Mesopotamia lay between them.

geo.q: Which river flows through Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade?
geo.why: The Danube flows through ten countries and four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

geo.q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
geo.why: The Volga, about 3,500 km long, flows through Russia to the Caspian Sea.

geo.q: Which river flows through Paris?
geo.why: The Seine flows through Paris to the English Channel.

geo.q: Which river flows through London?
geo.why: The Thames flows through London to the North Sea.

geo.q: Which great river flows through six countries, from Tibet to Vietnam?
geo.why: The Mekong flows from Tibet through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand and Cambodia to Vietnam.

geo.q: Which African river crosses the equator twice?
geo.why: The Congo, Africa's deepest river, crosses the equator twice on its way to the Atlantic.

geo.q: Victoria Falls lies on which river?
geo.why: Victoria Falls, on the Zambezi, lies on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe.

geo.q: Which river gave Niger and Nigeria their names?
geo.why: The Niger flows in a great arc through Guinea, Mali, Niger and Nigeria.

geo.q: On the border of which two countries is Mount Everest?
geo.why: Everest, 8,849 m, the world's highest mountain, sits on the border of Nepal and China's Tibet.

geo.q: Which country is home to Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain?
geo.why: Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m, is a volcano in northern Tanzania, near the Kenyan border.

geo.q: Which is the highest mountain in the Americas?
geo.why: Aconcagua, 6,961 m, in Argentina's Andes, is the highest mountain outside Asia.

geo.q: Which mountain range covers much of Switzerland and Austria?
geo.why: The Alps arc across France, Italy, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria and Slovenia.

geo.q: Which mountains separate France from Spain?
geo.why: The Pyrenees run along the border of France and Spain; tiny Andorra sits high in them.

geo.q: Which mountains are often said to divide Europe from Asia?
geo.why: The Ural Mountains run north to south through Russia and mark a traditional border of Europe and Asia.

geo.q: Which is the longest mountain range on land?
geo.why: The Andes run about 7,000 km down the west of South America.

geo.q: Which mountains run across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia?
geo.why: The Atlas Mountains run across northwest Africa, separating the Mediterranean coast from the Sahara.

geo.q: Which is Japan's highest mountain?
geo.why: Mount Fuji, 3,776 m, is a volcano near Tokyo and a symbol of Japan.

geo.q: Europe's most active large volcano, Etna, is on which island?
geo.why: Mount Etna, on Sicily, Italy, is one of the world's most active volcanoes.

geo.q: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
geo.why: The Sahara covers about 9 million km² of North Africa, nearly the size of the United States.

geo.q: Which desert covers much of southern Mongolia and northern China?
geo.why: The Gobi is a cold desert in Mongolia and northern China, famous for dinosaur fossils.

geo.q: Which is the driest non-polar desert on Earth?
geo.why: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert have had almost no rain for centuries.

geo.q: Which is the largest ocean?
geo.why: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface, more than all the land combined.

geo.q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
geo.why: The Indian Ocean lies between Africa, Asia and Australia.

geo.q: Which ocean lies between Europe and North America?
geo.why: The Atlantic separates the Americas from Europe and Africa.

geo.q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
geo.why: Lake Baikal in Siberia is over 1,600 m deep and holds about a fifth of the world's fresh surface water.

geo.q: Which is the largest lake in the world by area?
geo.why: The Caspian Sea, bordered by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan, is the largest lake on Earth.

geo.q: Which is Africa's largest lake?
geo.why: Lake Victoria is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania; the White Nile flows out of it.

geo.q: Which is the lowest point on land?
a: The shore of the Dead Sea
geo.why: The Dead Sea shore, on the border of Jordan and Israel, is about 430 m below sea level.

geo.q: Which canal links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea?
geo.why: The Suez Canal in Egypt, opened in 1869, lets ships sail between Europe and Asia without going round Africa.

geo.q: Which canal links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans?
geo.why: The Panama Canal, opened in 1914, cuts across Panama between the Atlantic and Pacific.

geo.q: Which narrow strait divides Istanbul between Europe and Asia?
geo.why: The Bosporus runs through Istanbul, so the city lies on two continents.

geo.q: Which strait separates Spain from Morocco?
geo.why: The Strait of Gibraltar is only 14 km wide at its narrowest, between Europe and Africa.

geo.q: Which strait, between Iran and Oman, carries about a fifth of the world's oil?
geo.why: About a fifth of the world's oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf.

geo.q: Off which country's coast is the Great Barrier Reef?
geo.why: The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, runs along Queensland in northeast Australia.

geo.q: In which country is Machu Picchu?
geo.why: Machu Picchu, an Inca citadel from the 1400s, sits high in the Andes of Peru.

geo.q: In which country is the Taj Mahal?
geo.why: The Taj Mahal, in Agra, India, was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife.

geo.q: In which country is Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world?
geo.why: Angkor Wat was built in the 1100s by the Khmer Empire; it appears on Cambodia's flag.

geo.q: In which country is Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock?
geo.why: Petra was the capital of the Nabataeans, carved into cliffs in southern Jordan over 2,000 years ago.

geo.q: Which city is famous for the Christ the Redeemer statue?
geo.why: Christ the Redeemer has overlooked Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, from Corcovado mountain since 1931.

geo.q: In which country is the Maya city of Chichén Itzá?
geo.why: Chichén Itzá, with its step pyramid, is on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

geo.q: Which country built the Great Wall?
geo.why: China built walls along its northern frontier for over 2,000 years; most of what stands today is from the Ming dynasty.

geo.q: In which city is the Colosseum?
geo.why: The Colosseum in Rome held up to about 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights.

geo.q: In which city is the Parthenon?
geo.why: The Parthenon, a temple to Athena, stands on the Acropolis above Athens.

geo.q: Which is the smallest country in the world?
geo.why: Vatican City, home of the Pope, covers less than half a square kilometre inside Rome.

geo.q: Which city stands on two continents?
geo.why: Istanbul lies on both banks of the Bosporus, in Europe and Asia.

geo.q: Which country's capital is Amsterdam, though its government sits in The Hague?
geo.why: Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands, but the parliament and government sit in The Hague.

geo.q: Which country has two capitals, La Paz and Sucre?
geo.why: Sucre is Bolivia's constitutional capital; La Paz is the seat of government and the world's highest capital, at about 3,600 m.

geo.q: Which country has three capital cities?
geo.why: South Africa has three: Pretoria (government), Cape Town (parliament) and Bloemfontein (courts).

geo.q: What is the capital of Australia?
geo.why: Canberra was built as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne and became the capital in 1913.

geo.q: What is the capital of Canada?
geo.why: Ottawa, on the border of Ontario and Quebec, was chosen as Canada's capital by Queen Victoria in 1857.

geo.q: What is the capital of Brazil?
geo.why: Brasília, built from scratch in the interior, replaced Rio de Janeiro as Brazil's capital in 1960.

geo.q: What is the capital of Turkey?
geo.why: Ankara became Turkey's capital in 1923; Istanbul is the largest city.

geo.q: What is the capital of Nigeria?
geo.why: Abuja, in the centre of Nigeria, replaced Lagos as the capital in 1991.

geo.q: Which is the largest city in the world, counting its whole metropolitan area?
geo.why: Greater Tokyo has about 37 million people, though Delhi, Shanghai and Jakarta are catching up.

geo.q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
geo.why: Russia covers about 17 million km², spanning 11 time zones.

geo.q: Which country has the longest coastline?
geo.why: Canada has the world's longest coastline, over 200,000 km, thanks to its Arctic islands.

geo.q: Which country has the most islands?
geo.why: Sweden has the most islands, over 260,000, though most are tiny and uninhabited; Indonesia has about 17,000.

geo.q: Which is the largest island in the world?
geo.why: Greenland is the largest island; Australia is counted as a continent.

geo.q: Which country has the largest Muslim population?
geo.why: Indonesia has about 240 million Muslims, more than any other country.

geo.q: Which country is long and thin, stretching about 4,300 km down South America's west coast?
geo.why: Chile is about 4,300 km long but on average only about 175 km wide.

geo.q: Which is the largest landlocked country?
geo.why: Kazakhstan, about 2.7 million km², is the largest country with no coast on the open ocean.

geo.q: Which is the lowest-lying country in the world?
geo.why: The Maldives averages about 1.5 m above sea level, making it highly vulnerable to rising seas.

geo.q: Which is the most densely populated country?
geo.why: Monaco squeezes about 38,000 people into 2 km².

geo.q: Which is the only country that is also a whole continent?
geo.why: Australia is the only country that covers an entire continent; Antarctica has no country of its own.

geo.q: How many continents are there, by the most common count?
geo.why: The usual count is seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Europe, North America and South America.

geo.q: Which is the largest continent?
geo.why: Asia covers about 30% of Earth's land and holds about 60% of its people.

geo.q: Which continent has the most countries?
geo.why: Africa has 54 countries, more than any other continent.

geo.q: Which is the only continent with no permanent residents?
geo.why: Antarctica has only scientists who come and go; no one lives there for good.

geo.q: Which line divides Earth into the Northern and Southern hemispheres?
geo.why: The equator, at 0° latitude, divides north from south; the Prime Meridian through Greenwich divides east from west.

geo.q: Through which London district does the Prime Meridian, 0° longitude, run?
geo.why: Since 1884 the Prime Meridian has run through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, London.

geo.q: Which country is named after the line that runs through it?
geo.why: Ecuador is Spanish for "equator", which crosses the country just north of Quito.

geo.q: What is the main language of Brazil?
geo.why: Brazil speaks Portuguese, from its time as a Portuguese colony; it is the largest Portuguese-speaking country.

geo.q: Which country has the most Spanish speakers?
geo.why: Mexico has about 130 million Spanish speakers, more than twice as many as Spain.

geo.q: Which country has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh?
geo.why: Switzerland has four national languages; German is the most widely spoken.

geo.q: Which two main languages are spoken in Belgium?
geo.why: Belgium is split between Dutch-speaking Flanders in the north and French-speaking Wallonia in the south.

geo.q: Which two languages are official across Canada?
geo.why: English and French are Canada's official languages; most French speakers live in Quebec.

geo.q: Which language has the most native speakers in India?
geo.why: Hindi is the most widely spoken language in India; the country has 22 official languages.

geo.q: Which language is mainly spoken in Iran?
geo.why: Iranians mainly speak Persian, or Farsi, not Arabic.

geo.q: What is the main language of Argentina?
geo.why: Argentina speaks Spanish, though many Argentines have Italian ancestors.

geo.q: Which two languages are official in the Philippines?
geo.why: Filipino, based on Tagalog, and English are the official languages of the Philippines.

geo.q: Which is the most populous country in Africa?
geo.why: Nigeria has over 220 million people, the most in Africa.

geo.q: Which country has the fourth-largest population in the world?
geo.why: Indonesia, with about 280 million people, comes after India, China and the United States.

geo.q: Which country is made up mainly of a North Island and a South Island?
geo.why: New Zealand is mainly two big islands, North Island and South Island.

geo.q: Which large island lies off the southeast coast of Africa?
geo.why: Madagascar, the fourth-largest island, split from India about 88 million years ago; most of its wildlife lives nowhere else.

geo.q: Which island country lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two plates are pulling apart?
geo.why: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which is why it has so many volcanoes and hot springs.

geo.q: Which country is shaped like a boot?
geo.why: Italy's boot-shaped peninsula reaches into the Mediterranean, with Sicily at its toe.

geo.q: Which country completely surrounds Lesotho?
geo.why: Lesotho is entirely surrounded by South Africa; San Marino and Vatican City are surrounded by Italy.

geo.q: Which island city-state lies at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula?
geo.why: Singapore sits at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, on one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

geo.q: Greenland is a self-governing part of which country?
geo.why: Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.

geo.q: Which country borders North Korea to the south?
geo.why: The Korean Demilitarized Zone separates North and South Korea, roughly along the 38th parallel.

geo.q: Which US state is made up of islands in the Pacific?
geo.why: Hawaii, a chain of volcanic islands, became the 50th US state in 1959.

geo.q: Which country sold Alaska to the United States in 1867?
geo.why: The US bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for $7.2 million.

geo.q: Which country lies just 14 km from Spain, across the Strait of Gibraltar?
geo.why: Morocco faces Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar.

geo.q: Which two South American countries are landlocked?
geo.why: Bolivia and Paraguay are South America's only landlocked countries.

geo.q: Which country lies between Russia and China and has the lowest population density of any country?
geo.why: Mongolia has about 3.5 million people in an area larger than Western Europe.

geo.q: In which city is the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building?
geo.why: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, is 828 m tall.

geo.q: Which country is famous for its fjords and the midnight sun?
geo.why: Norway's coast is cut by deep fjords, carved by glaciers; in its far north the summer sun never sets.

geo.q: Which country owns the Galápagos Islands, where Darwin studied evolution?
geo.why: The Galápagos Islands, in the Pacific about 1,000 km off the coast, belong to Ecuador.

geo.q: Which four countries make up the United Kingdom?
a: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
Great Britain, Ireland, Wales and Scotland
geo.why: The UK is England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; the Republic of Ireland is a separate country.
